title: Social-network use is near-universal among young Europeans, but the age and country gaps reveal different digital social worlds
source_unit: Eurostat, EU survey on the use of ICT in households and by individuals: online social-network use in 2025
geography: European Union; people aged 16-29 and general population aged 16-74 across EU Member States

observations.period: 2025; EU age gradient in social-network use

denominator.unit: EU survey respondents aged 16-29 and general population aged 16-74; source article reports shares without pooled respondent count

youth_social_network_use.unit: percent of EU residents aged 16-29 using social networks

general_social_network_use.unit: percent of EU residents aged 16-74 using social networks

youth_general_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between 16-29 and 16-74 social-network use

countries_over_90_percent_youth.unit: EU Member States where more than 90% of 16-29-year-olds used social networks

mechanism.value: Social-network participation is a near-default social infrastructure for young Europeans, while the age gap means institutions, markets, and cultural life are encountered through different digital social environments across generations

observations.method: Eurostat EU ICT household and individual survey indicator; social-network use includes creating a profile, posting messages, or making other contributions.
observations.uncertainty: The measure captures participation in social networks during the reference period, not intensity, platform mix, passive viewing, content quality, social support, political influence, or consumer outcomes.
observations.subgroup: EU residents aged 16-29 compared with the general population aged 16-74; the age ranges are not identical populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: High social-network use may reflect required communication, entertainment, or platform migration rather than stronger community, wellbeing, or civic capacity.

denominator.unit: EU Member State survey estimates for people aged 16-29; source article reports percentages without pooled respondent count

cyprus_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Cyprus using social networks

czechia_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Czechia using social networks

denmark_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Denmark using social networks

finland_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Finland using social networks

italy_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Italy using social networks

germany_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Germany using social networks

luxembourg_youth_use.unit: percent of 16-29-year-olds in Luxembourg using social networks

mechanism.value: A common European age trend sits on top of national digital-social ecologies: infrastructure, culture, language, platform availability, and use norms can produce different youth participation levels

observations.method: Eurostat comparison of Member State estimates from the EU ICT household and individual survey.
observations.uncertainty: Country differences are descriptive and do not identify the contribution of broadband quality, education, income, language, platform mix, or survey response patterns; they are not causal country rankings.
observations.subgroup: People aged 16-29 in EU Member States, with country estimates reported by Eurostat.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower reported use may indicate alternative communication practices, different definitions or survey interpretations, or lower platform participation without lower social connection.

denominator.unit: Country-level estimates for people aged 16-74 and 16-29; source article reports selected comparisons without pooled respondent count

largest_age_gap_croatia.unit: percentage-point gap between general population and 16-29-year-olds in Croatia

largest_age_gap_austria.unit: percentage-point gap between general population and 16-29-year-olds in Austria

largest_age_gap_poland.unit: percentage-point gap between general population and 16-29-year-olds in Poland

smallest_age_gap_denmark.unit: percentage-point gap between general population and 16-29-year-olds in Denmark

smallest_age_gap_malta.unit: percentage-point gap between general population and 16-29-year-olds in Malta

smallest_age_gap_cyprus.unit: percentage-point gap between general population and 16-29-year-olds in Cyprus

mechanism.value: The same headline of youth social-network adoption can imply different generational divides: in some countries youth use is an extension of broad population use, while in others it marks a sharper age-specific platform transition

observations.method: Eurostat age-gap comparison using the same 2025 social-network indicator across EU Member States.
observations.uncertainty: The selected country gaps do not explain why age gradients differ and cannot establish a causal relationship between national context and youth adoption.
observations.subgroup: Young people aged 16-29 and general population aged 16-74 in selected EU Member States.
observations.counterinterpretation: A small age gap can mean older adults also use social networks extensively, not that youth participation is less socially important; a large gap can reflect cohort replacement rather than exclusion.

related_sources.claim: Eurostat's source dataset provides the underlying social-network-use indicator for EU countries and age groups.
Eurostat's digital-economy statistics provide methodological and comparative context for ICT use by households and individuals.

boundary: This record adds EU statistical evidence on social-network participation, age gradients, and country variation. It does not measure time spent, platform-specific exposure, content, social connection quality, mental health, political influence, consumer behavior, or causal digital inequality.
